newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Belarus leader defies OSCE critics on democracy.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader defies OSCE critics on democracy.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, responding to criticism at a European security summit, defended his country's record on democracy on Monday and defiantly warned other countries not to interfere.
Lukashenko also blasted NATO plans to expand eastwards up to the border of Belarus, singled out the United States for criticism and denied there was a political crisis in his former Soviet republic.

"It would be counterproductive to try to exert pressure on us or try to interfere in our internal affairs," Lukashenko told the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) meeting in Lisbon.
"We expect from the OSCE the corresponding attitude and compliance with the existing rules and procedures governing its relations with states participating in the organisation."

Lukashenko attended the OSCE summit of more than 50 nations despite recent criticism by Western leaders of his increasingly authoritarian rule, and found himself isolated under a barrage of fresh criticism at the start of the two-day meeting.
Critics have suggested that a referendum on November 24, in which Lukashenko won backing for strengthening his powers, was neither free nor fair.

The Portuguese hosts in Lisbon greeted Lukashenko coolly with formal handshakes and few words. Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, chairman in office of the OSCE, told the summit he was "deeply concerned" by developments in Belarus.

U.S. Vice President Al Gore, standing in for President Bill Clinton, also voiced concern. Leaders of Poland, Ukraine and Lithuania, which border Belarus, met in Lisbon on Sunday to discuss the situation and called for democracy in the region.
But Lukashenko defended the much-criticised referendum and his handling of a crisis in which his opponents in parliament had threatened to try to impeach him.

He said the country of 10 million people, which has been independent only since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and is again seeking closer integration with Moscow, had solved its problems democratically.

"The recent referendum held in Belarus was held in full compliance with the constitution and legislation of our country. Any attempt to represent the results as not legitimate are completely without foundation," Lukashenko said.

"I emphasise strongly that we do not have a political crisis and there is no hint of a division in our society, despite what out internal opposition would have you believe. Since the referendum, there has been peace and stability in our society."

Hitting back at Washington, one of his fiercest critics, Lukashenko said: "This statement is addressed to all those who wish to get to grips with what is going on in Belarus, including the United States of America."
Lukashenko supported the general principles of the OSCE, saying Belarus would strive to follow its guidelines on democracy and security.
But he joined Russian President Viktor Chernomyrdin in condemning NATO's plans to take in other countries of eastern and central Europe.

"Perhaps we raise our voice against this louder than others because it is Belarus which would suffer most from a new split in Europe. In this case the dividing line will run along the border of Belarus," he said.
